newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Besieged S.Korean unionists make peace offer - TV.
newsitem.headline: Besieged S.Korean unionists make peace offer - TV.

text.p: South Korean union leaders sheltering from arrest in a Seoul cathedral will end "all-out" strikes and work stoppages will only take place once a week, Yonhap Television News reported on Saturday.

Separately, state television reported the leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions had offered to halt industrial action completely if the government agreed to delay implementation of a controversial labour law.
Riot police maintained a tight security net around Myongdong Cathedral on Saturday, with officers trained in unarmed combat guarding approaches to the church.
Witnesses said they checked passing cars in an apparent bid to stop union activists sneaking in or out.
A spokesman for the confederation, which has been spearheading more than three weeks of strikes, declined to confirm the television reports but said the group had decided to change tactics.
He said a change of tactics would be aimed at prolonging protests at the law, which allows firms to lay off workers and replace strikers. The law is due to go into effect in March.
"Our position will be announced in a news conference later today," he said.

The move followed unyielding pressure from the government on confederation leader Kwon Young-kil and six deputies sheltering at the cathedral from arrest. The government has vowed to crack down on wildcat strikes and arrest strike leaders.
President Kim Young-sam has said the law will not be revoked, arguing labour reform is vital to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.

The state-run Korea Broadcasting System said the offer to end strikes on condition the government delayed implementing the law was conveyed by South Korea's Roman Catholic cardinal Stephen Kim when he met President Kim on Friday.
The cardinal told reporters after he met the president he appealed to the government to end the industrial crisis through dialogue. He gave no further details.
Yonhap said unions would return to work on Monday and stoppages would take place only on Wednesday each week.
On Friday, the ruling New Korea Party scorned Kwon's acceptance of an offer for a televised debate over the law, saying it could not guarantee the safety of a fugitive.
Kwon was taking up party chairman Lee Hong-koo's own suggestion for a televised, round-table discussion between the ruling party leaders and unspecified union heads.
The New Korea Party called on unions to put forward more suitable candidates.
